title: How do you deploy and manage Kafka Connect — REST API to create/update/delete/pause/resume connectors, monitor via JMX metrics, handle failures with dead letter queue config (`errors.tolerance=all`, `errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name`)?
shortTitle: How do you deploy and manage Kafka Connect, and how do you handle connector failures?

s1_definition.profdef: You operate Kafka Connect in distributed mode entirely through its REST API, which exposes endpoints to create, read, update, delete, pause, resume, and restart connectors and their tasks, and to query status. You monitor it through JMX metrics that the workers expose, covering task state, throughput, and error rates, usually scraped into a metrics system. You handle bad records with error tolerance and a dead letter queue: setting error tolerance to all means the runtime skips records it cannot process instead of failing the task, and configuring a dead letter queue topic captures those skipped records with diagnostic headers so nothing is silently lost.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, managing Kafka Connect is like running the courier dispatch office through a single control desk, the REST API: you phone in to start a route, pause one during a storm, resume it later, or cancel it, and ask for the status of any van. The JMX metrics are the CCTV and dashboards showing which vans are moving, how fast, and how many parcels were damaged. The dead letter queue is a dedicated damaged-parcel shelf: when a parcel cannot be delivered, instead of the whole route grinding to a halt, the courier sets that one parcel on the shelf with a note explaining what went wrong, and the route keeps running.
s1_definition.oneliner: Drive Connect through its REST API, watch it with JMX metrics, and keep bad records from stalling tasks by setting error tolerance to all with a dead letter queue topic.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You operate Kafka Connect in distributed mode entirely through its REST API, which exposes endpoints to create, read, update, delete, pause, resume, and restart connectors and their tasks, and to query status. You monitor it through JMX metrics that the workers expose, covering task state, throughput, and error rates, usually scraped into a metrics system. You handle bad records with error tolerance and a dead letter queue: setting error tolerance to all means the runtime skips records it cannot process instead of failing the task, and configuring a dead letter queue topic captures those skipped records with diagnostic headers so nothing is silently lost.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, managing Kafka Connect is like running the courier dispatch office through a single control desk, the REST API: you phone in to start a route, pause one during a storm, resume it later, or cancel it, and ask for the status of any van. The JMX metrics are the CCTV and dashboards showing which vans are moving, how fast, and how many parcels were damaged. The dead letter queue is a dedicated damaged-parcel shelf: when a parcel cannot be delivered, instead of the whole route grinding to a halt, the courier sets that one parcel on the shelf with a note explaining what went wrong, and the route keeps running.

**One line to remember:** Drive Connect through its REST API, watch it with JMX metrics, and keep bad records from stalling tasks by setting error tolerance to all with a dead letter queue topic.

sections.s2_technical:
In distributed mode you never edit local files to manage connectors; you call the REST API on any worker, typically on port 8083, and the change propagates across the cluster through the internal config topic. To create or update a connector you put a JSON configuration to the connectors endpoint, for example a post to the connectors path with the connector name and config. To see what is running you get the connectors list, and to inspect one you get its status, which returns the connector state and each task's state and the worker hosting it. To stop and start you put to the pause and resume endpoints, and to recover a failed task you post to the restart endpoint, which is the common fix when a task has errored but the underlying problem is resolved.

Monitoring relies on the metrics the workers expose over JMX. The important ones are connector and task state, which tells you if anything is failed or paused, source and sink record rates for throughput, and error and retry counts. In production you export these with a JMX exporter into a metrics system and build dashboards and alerts, for example alerting when any task state is failed, when the sink record rate drops to zero unexpectedly, or when the dead letter queue rate climbs. You also watch consumer lag for sink connectors, because a sink falling behind means it is not keeping up with the topic.

Error handling is where Connect earns its keep in production, because a single bad record must not stall a task. The error tolerance setting controls this. The default, error tolerance none, means the first unprocessable record fails the task and the pipeline stops, which is safe but brittle. Setting error tolerance to all means the runtime tolerates failures in conversion and transformation and in the record itself, skipping the offending record and continuing. On its own, skipping would silently lose data, so you pair it with a dead letter queue: you configure a dead letter queue topic name, and the skipped records are routed there instead of being dropped, and you enable including their error context headers so each dead-lettered record carries why it failed.

The dead letter queue is specifically for sink connector record-level failures, such as a record that cannot be deserialized or written to the target. You give it a topic name, optionally set its replication factor, and turn on context headers so the record arrives with the original topic, partition, offset, and the exception. Then you build a triage or replay process around that topic. The senior nuances are that error tolerance all plus a dead letter queue converts a hard stop into a soft, observable skip, which is usually what you want for a resilient pipeline, but you must monitor the dead letter queue or it silently accumulates lost money events; that this covers record-level errors, while infrastructure failures like the target being down are handled by task retries and restarts, not the dead letter queue; that you should secure the REST API because it can create and delete connectors; and that connector configurations should be version-controlled and applied through automation rather than ad hoc curl calls, so the cluster's state is reproducible.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem at National Bank of India is that a sink connector archiving transactions to storage kept failing the whole task on a single malformed record, and the operations team had no clean way to manage and observe the pipeline.

Problem 1 — one bad transaction record with an unparseable field failed the entire sink task, so the whole archive stopped and a backlog built up. This is exactly what error tolerance all plus a dead letter queue solves: the bad record is routed aside and the task keeps archiving everything else.

Problem 2 — the team needed to pause the pipeline during a storage maintenance window and resume it afterwards, without redeploying anything. This is exactly what the REST API pause and resume endpoints provide.

Problem 3 — when a task did fail for an infrastructure reason, they needed to see it and restart it quickly. This is exactly what status plus the restart endpoint, backed by JMX metrics and alerts, provides.

The code will model a `ConnectRestApi` offering create, status, pause, resume, and restart, a `SinkTask` that processes records with error tolerance and routes bad ones to a `DeadLetterQueue`, and a `JmxMetrics` collector tracking processed, dead-lettered, and task state. The demo step is: create the connector, process a batch containing one poison record so it is dead-lettered while the rest succeed, read the metrics, pause and resume during maintenance, then simulate a task failure and restart it.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql
-- The sink writes archived rows here (or to S3); dead-lettered rows are inspected later.
CREATE TABLE archived_txns (
    txn_id     VARCHAR(30) PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    archived_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# connectors/txn-s3-sink.json (submitted via REST API)
# { "name":"txn-s3-sink",
#   "config":{
#     "connector.class":"io.confluent.connect.s3.S3SinkConnector",
#     "topics":"bank.transactions","s3.bucket.name":"nbi-txn-archive",
#     "errors.tolerance":"all",                                  # skip bad records
#     "errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name":"bank.transactions.dlq",# route them here
#     "errors.deadletterqueue.context.headers.enable":"true",    # why it failed
#     "errors.deadletterqueue.topic.replication.factor":"3" } }
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the model demo
javac com/bank/connectops/demo/ConnectOpsDemo.java
java com.bank.connectops.demo.ConnectOpsDemo

# Real REST lifecycle (distributed mode):
curl -X POST http://worker1:8083/connectors -d @connectors/txn-s3-sink.json \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
curl http://worker1:8083/connectors/txn-s3-sink/status
curl -X PUT http://worker1:8083/connectors/txn-s3-sink/pause
curl -X PUT http://worker1:8083/connectors/txn-s3-sink/resume
curl -X POST http://worker1:8083/connectors/txn-s3-sink/tasks/0/restart
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a batch of three transaction records, one of which is malformed, flowing through a sink task configured with error tolerance all and a dead letter queue, all managed via the REST API.

Step 1: The operator posts the connector configuration to the REST API. The runtime creates the connector and the task moves to running, and the metrics show the task state as running.

Step 2: The sink task processes the batch. The first record for Rajesh is valid, so it is archived and the processed metric increments.

Step 3: The second record is malformed and throws during processing. Because error tolerance is all, the task does not fail; instead it routes the bad record to the dead letter queue topic with context headers explaining the failure, and the dead-lettered metric increments. The task keeps running.

Step 4: The third record for Priya is valid and archived normally, proving the single bad record did not stall the pipeline.

Step 5: The operator reads the JMX metrics, seeing two records processed, one dead-lettered, and the task still running. Then, for a storage maintenance window, the operator pauses the connector via the REST API and later resumes it, with no redeploy.

Step 6: Finally an infrastructure error puts the task into a failed state. The operator queries status, sees failed, and posts a task restart, after which status returns running again. The output shows the archive of good records, the dead letter routing, the metrics, the pause and resume, and the failure and restart.

sections.s6_takeaway:
I operate Kafka Connect in distributed mode entirely through its REST API, never by editing local files. The API lets me create and update a connector by sending its JSON configuration, list and inspect connectors and their task status, pause and resume a connector, delete it, and restart a failed task, and because it runs on every worker and stores state in Kafka internal topics, a change I make on one worker propagates across the whole cluster. In practice I keep connector configurations version-controlled and apply them through automation so the cluster's state is reproducible rather than a pile of ad hoc commands.

For monitoring I rely on the JMX metrics the workers expose, especially connector and task state so I know if anything is failed or paused, source and sink record rates for throughput, sink consumer lag, and the dead letter queue rate. I export these into a metrics system and alert on a failed task state, on a sink rate unexpectedly dropping to zero, and on a climbing dead letter queue rate.

The failure handling is the part interviewers really want. By default error tolerance is none, so the first unprocessable record fails the task and stops the pipeline, which is safe but brittle. In production I set error tolerance to all, which tells the runtime to skip records it cannot convert, transform, or write, and I pair that with a dead letter queue topic and enable context headers, so every skipped record is routed to that topic carrying its original topic, partition, offset, and the exception, instead of being silently dropped.

At National Bank of India this fixed a real incident where one malformed transaction record was failing the entire archive task and building a backlog. After setting error tolerance to all with a dead letter queue, that single bad record went to the dead letter topic with its error context while the rest of the transactions kept archiving, and we built a triage and replay process around the dead letter topic. The senior nuances I add are that this converts a hard stop into a soft, observable skip, which is what you want for resilience, but you must monitor the dead letter queue or it silently accumulates lost events; that the dead letter queue handles record-level errors while infrastructure failures like the target being down are handled by task retries and a restart, not the dead letter queue; and that the REST API must be secured because it can create and delete connectors across the cluster.

---

keyPoints: Kafka Connect: move data between Kafka and external systems
Source connector: DB/file -> Kafka. Sink connector: Kafka -> DB/file
Debezium: CDC (Change Data Capture) source connector
Distributed mode: scalable, fault-tolerant connector deployment
